full_item_before.statement: Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ in branch (a) and the Axiom of Choice together with $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ as declared by its weak-solvability lemmas in branch (b) ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $c>0$ and let $(\varphi,A)$ be a potential pair of the framework ([[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]], [[def-em-fields]]) with field pair $(E,B)$ and Lorenz divergence $G=\operatorname{div}A+c^{-2}\partial_t\varphi$. (a) [All-space slab; Lorenz gauge] Let $t_0<T$ and let $(\varphi,A)$ be of class $C^\infty$ in the extension sense on $\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]$ (the restriction of a $C^\infty$ pair on $\mathbb R^3\times J$ for some open interval $J\supset[t_0,T]$; [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). Then there is a gauge function $\chi$ of class $C^\infty$ in the extension sense on $\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]$ with $\chi(\cdot,t_0)=0$, $\partial_t\chi(\cdot,t_0)=0$ and $W\chi=G$ on $\mathbb R^3\times(t_0,T)$; the transformed pair $T_\chi(\varphi,A)$ is in Lorenz gauge on $\mathbb R^3\times(t_0,T)$, has the same field pair $(E,B)$, and any two such gauge functions differ by a solution of $W\chi=0$. This is the exact content of [[lem-em-gauge-wave-reachability]] read for potential pairs of the framework; its physical content is that every smooth potential representation of a field pair on a slab admits a Lorenz-gauge representative with zero gauge Cauchy data at $t_0$, without changing the fields. (b) [Bounded smooth domain; Coulomb gauge] Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded $C^\infty$ domain ([[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]), let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval and let $(\varphi,A)$ be of class $C^\infty$ on a neighbourhood of $\bar\Omega\times\bar I$. Fix a smooth time-independent Dirichlet datum $g\in C^\infty(\partial\Omega)$. Then there is a gauge function $\psi$, of class $C^\infty$ on a neighbourhood of $\bar\Omega\times\bar I$, with $\psi(\cdot,t)|_{\partial\Omega}=g$ for every $t\in I$, such that $$\operatorname{div}(A+\nabla\psi)(\cdot,t)=0\qquad\text{on }\Omega\text{ for every }t\in I;$$ the transformed pair $T_\psi(\varphi,A)$ is in Coulomb gauge on $\Omega\times I$ and has the same field pair $(E,B)$ ([[pthm-em-gauge-invariance]]). The generator is unique among such generators with datum $g$; if $g=0$, then $\psi$ is the unique generator with zero boundary values. (c) [Residual freedom on star-shaped domains] Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and star-shaped ([[def-star-shaped-open-subset-of-rn]]) and let $(\varphi,A)$, $(\tilde\varphi,\tilde A)$ be two potential pairs of class $C^2$ jointly on $\Omega\times I$ ([[def-interval]]) with the same field pair, both in Lorenz gauge. Then there is a gauge function $\chi$ of class $C^2$ jointly with $(\tilde\varphi,\tilde A)=T_\chi(\varphi,A)$ and $W\chi=0$ on $\Omega\times I$. (d) [Scope] Nothing is asserted about gauge functions meeting arbitrary prescribed boundary or initial restrictions: in (a) the gauge function has zero Cauchy data at $t_0$ and no spatial boundary condition or decay, and $\Omega$ is all of $\mathbb R^3$; in (b) the datum is the fixed time-independent Dirichlet datum $g$ and the Neumann variant with its own compatibility condition for every $t$ is not claimed; the older promise of a global Lorenz gauge on a bounded domain with prescribed boundary data is explicitly outside this result. The Coulomb-gauge statement concerns the spatial divergence in the chosen inertial chart, and the instantaneous appearance of the Coulomb potential is a property of the representation, not a signal: only the field pair $(E,B)$ is physical content ([[def-em-fields]]).

full_item_before.physical_scope: Gauge reachability for potential representations of the classical vacuum electromagnetic framework, in exactly two declared branches: the all-space smooth slab branch, where a Lorenz-gauge representative with zero gauge Cauchy data exists (carrying countable choice through the wave supplier), and the bounded smooth-domain branch, where a Coulomb-gauge representative with a prescribed time-independent smooth Dirichlet datum exists and is unique (carrying the choice assumptions declared by the elliptic supplier). The item also classifies residual freedom on star-shaped domains. It makes no empirical claim, asserts nothing about arbitrary prescribed boundary or initial restrictions, and does not claim that gauge conditions are physically observable.

Prescribe either (i) a Dirichlet family $g_D(p,t)$ smooth in boundary charts on a neighbourhood of $\partial\Omega\times\overline I$, or (ii) an outward conormal family $\kappa(p,t)$ with the same smoothness and the compatibility $\int_{\Omega_j}\varepsilon_0\operatorname{div}A(\cdot,t)\,dx+\int_{\partial\Omega_j}\kappa(\cdot,t)\,dS=0$ for every connected component $\Omega_j$ and every $t\in I$. new_earlier_mathematical_items.title: A fixed smooth-domain extension that preserves smooth parameters
new_earlier_mathematical_items.statement:
Let `Omega⊂R3` be a bounded smooth graph domain. Choose an open spatial neighbourhood `V` of its compact closure. There exists a fixed real linear spatial extension operator `E_Omega`, determined only by the domain, finite charts and cutoffs, with this parameter property. For every open interval `J` and function `u:Omega×J→R` that is smooth in the interior and whose every mixed derivative has a continuous extension to `closure Omega × J`, the function `E_Omega u` is `C∞` on `R3×J`, equals `u` and all its continuous boundary jets on `closure Omega × J`, and is supported spatially in one fixed compact subset of `V`. For every compact `K⊂J`, integer `m≥0` and `j≥0`,

$$\sup_{t\in K}\|\partial_t^j E_\Omega u(\cdot,t)\|_{C^m(\mathbb R^3)}\le C_m\sup_{t\in K}\|\partial_t^j u(\cdot,t)\|_{C^m(\overline\Omega)}.$$

The `C^m` seminorm is the finite sum of suprema of spatial derivatives through order `m`. The extension commutes with every time derivative; charts and coefficients do not depend on `t`. No uniform bound over all of an unbounded `J` is assumed. Vector-valued inputs of finite dimension are extended componentwise. This construction adds no choice principle: a finite atlas can be selected from the cover of all admissible chart patches, finite cutoffs are supplied by the published finite-partition/cutoff lemmas, and the infinite coefficient sequence is defined explicitly below. The consuming elliptic/Sobolev argument retains its already-declared AC assumptions.
new_earlier_mathematical_items.strategy:
**1. Explicit coefficients; no unproved moment lemma.** Put `b_k=−2^k`, `k=0,1,...`. For `N≥k` define

$$a_k^{(N)}=\prod_{\substack{0\le j\le N\\j\ne k}}\frac{1-b_j}{b_k-b_j},\qquad a_k=\lim_{N\to\infty}a_k^{(N)}.$$

The factors for `j<k` have sign negative, those for `j>k` positive; the sign is `(-1)^k`. For every finite index set, `prod(1+2^{-j})≤6`: the factors `j=0,1` give 3, and for the tail `j≥2`, the sum of `2^{-j}` is at most `1/2`, while the elementary induction `prod(1+x_j)≤1/(1−sum x_j)` bounds that tail by 2. Similarly `prod_{l=1}^M(1−2^{-l})≥1/4`: separate the first factor `1/2`, and use `prod(1−x_j)≥1−sum x_j≥1/2` on `l≥2`. The geometric-series supplier gives the stated sums, including their starting indices.

For `j<k` the absolute product is

$$2^{-k(k+1)/2}\frac{\prod_{j<k}(1+2^{-j})}{\prod_{l=1}^{k}(1-2^{-l})};$$

for `j>k` it is `prod_{j=k+1}^N(1+2^{-j})/prod_{l=1}^{N-k}(1−2^{-l})`. Thus

$$|a_k^{(N)}|\le576\,2^{-k(k+1)/2}\qquad(N\ge k).$$

At fixed `k`, the positive absolute value increases with `N`, since every new tail factor is greater than one, and it is bounded by this displayed constant. The published real monotone convergence theorem gives the limit `a_k`, with the same bound and sign. This defines every coefficient without selecting unspecified sequences.

For each integer `r≥0`, finite interpolation gives `sum_{k=0}^N a_k^{(N)} b_k^r=1` when `N≥r`: the polynomial

$$z^r-\sum_{k=0}^N b_k^r\prod_{\substack{0\le j\le N\\j\ne k}}\frac{z-b_j}{b_k-b_j}$$

has degree at most `N` and vanishes at the `N+1` distinct nodes `b_0,...,b_N`, so is zero by the exact published real-polynomial root bound; evaluate at `z=1`. To pass to the limit, the bound above gives `|a_k^{(N)} b_k^r|≤576·2^{-k(k+1)/2+kr}` uniformly in `N`. For `k≥2r+1` this is at most `576·2^{-k}`, whose tail tends to zero. First cut the sum at a fixed `M`, pass to the limit in those finitely many coefficients, and then let `M` increase. This proves both

$$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}a_k b_k^r=1,\qquad\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}|a_k|\,|b_k|^r<\infty\quad(r\ge0).$$

No original Seeley coefficient existence assertion is used as an unproved prerequisite.

**2. One flattened patch, with arbitrary parameters.** Write a smooth boundary patch as `(y,s)`, `s>0` inside the domain. A localized input `w(y,s,t)` has spatial support compactly inside the ambient chart, separated from its artificial edges, and every mixed derivative extends continuously to `s=0`. Extend it by zero at the artificial positive-side edges to the half-space. Choose a fixed smooth real normal cutoff `rho` that equals 1 near 0 and vanishes for `s≥delta/2`, with `delta` small enough that all sampled positive collar points remain in the chart. Define

$$\mathcal Ew(y,s,t)=w(y,s,t)\ (s\ge0),\qquad\mathcal Ew(y,s,t)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}a_k\rho(b_ks)w(y,b_ks,t)\ (s<0).$$

For fixed negative `s`, the sum is locally finite because `b_k s=2^k|s|` eventually exceeds the cutoff support. It is therefore smooth off `s=0`. For any normal order `r`, tangential multi-index `alpha`, time order `j`, and compact parameter/tangential set, its termwise derivative for `s<0` is

$$a_k b_k^r\,[\partial_z^r\partial_y^\alpha\partial_t^j(\rho(z)w(y,z,t))]_{z=b_ks}.$$

On the fixed compact collar and a compact `K⊂J`, every input derivative in this formula is bounded; the supremum of the sum is bounded by a finite cutoff-dependent constant times `sum|a_k||b_k|^r`. The bounds hold locally uniformly up to `s=0`, with the **same** compact time set `K`; only the normal spatial argument is sampled.

As `s↑0`, for each fixed term the normal cutoff is identically one and all its positive-order derivatives vanish. The derivative therefore tends to `a_k b_k^r partial_s^r partial_y^alpha partial_t^j w(y,0,t)`. The finite-head/uniform-tail argument using the weighted absolute sum proves uniform convergence of the boundary limit on compact `(y,t)` sets. The moment identity then makes that limit exactly the input boundary derivative. This establishes matching continuous derivatives of every mixed order; no derivative of an infinite nonuniformly convergent series is assumed at the boundary.

**3. Matching jets imply actual joint smoothness.** For a function glued from the two sides, matching values give continuity. If the side first partial derivatives extend continuously and agree, the normal coordinate-segment FTC, on either side and up to `s=0`, proves the derivative at `s=0` equals their common limit. For tangential or time segments at `s=0`, first write the coordinate-segment FTC at `s≠0`, then let `s→0`; uniform convergence on the compact segment passes the integral to the common continuous boundary derivative. FTC again gives that tangential/time derivative on `s=0`. Thus the glued function is `C1` jointly. Apply the same argument successively to the already-matched derivatives of orders 1,2,... to obtain `C∞` on the ambient patch × `J`. The input itself obeys those boundary segment identities by the same limit from its positive side. This is a complete smooth-gluing argument, not a reference to a Whitney extension theorem.

The derivative bound at total spatial order `m` uses only input derivatives through `m`, with `sum|a_k|2^{km}` finite and the fixed cutoff derivatives through `m`. The operator is linear and does not change the time argument, so the time-commutation identity and the stated local seminorm estimate follow.

**4. Finite chart gluing on the fixed smooth domain.** Choose finitely many shrunk smooth graph charts covering the compact boundary, an interior patch, and a finite smooth ambient partition equal to one near the domain closure. Localize `u` by these fixed spatial cutoffs. The interior piece is supported away from the physical boundary and is extended by zero, preserving smoothness. Each boundary piece is pulled through its smooth chart and extended by the preceding formula. Choose a fixed outer chart cutoff equal to one on both the positive localized support and the small negative support created by the extension, with compact support inside the larger chart; multiply before pulling back. This makes each piece smooth across its artificial edges when extended by zero in ambient space. Such collar sizes and cutoffs are available by shrinking the finite compact patches. The extension's tangential support never leaves that of the localized piece, and its negative normal support stays within `|s|<delta/2`, so the claimed outer support control is genuine.

Pullback is smooth by repeated ordinary chain rule with chart derivatives bounded at each fixed order on those compact supports. Add the finitely many pieces. On the domain their sum is `u` by the partition identity; all boundary jets agree by continuity from the interior. Each support lies in a fixed compact subset of the prescribed `V`, so their finite union does too. The charts, partitions and coefficient sequence are independent of time. This proves the claimed single parameter-preserving operator and its `C^m` seminorm bounds; it introduces no temporal patch choices or global bounds on unbounded intervals.

new_earlier_mathematical_items.title: Smooth parameter-dependent Dirichlet and compatible Neumann Poisson solvers
new_earlier_mathematical_items.statement:
Assume AC and Countable Choice carried by the variational/Sobolev suppliers. Let `Omega` be a bounded smooth graph domain in `R3`, `epsilon>0` constant and `J` an open interval. Let the bulk datum `f` be jointly smooth up to `closure Omega×J` in the all-mixed-derivative sense of the first supplier, and let boundary families `g_D`, `kappa` be smooth in a fixed finite boundary atlas × `J`. Then the Dirichlet problem `−epsilon Delta u=f`, `u|boundary=g_D` has a unique solution on `Omega×J`; it has a single smooth ambient continuation near the closed spatial domain × `J`. The Neumann problem `−epsilon Delta u=f`, `epsilon partial_nu u=kappa` has such a solution precisely when

$$\int_{\Omega_j}f(\cdot,t)+\int_{\partial\Omega_j}\kappa(\cdot,t)=0\quad\text{for each component and every }t\in J.$$

It is unique modulo a separately chosen spatial constant on each component at each time. The normalization `integral_Omega_j u(·,t)=0` gives a unique smooth family. Both solution operations are linear in their data; time differentiation commutes with them. Smoothness and estimates are local in compact time subintervals, with no uniform-in-`J` requirement. The smooth ambient continuations are auxiliary and are not unique off the closed physical spatial region.
new_earlier_mathematical_items.strategy:
**Fixed boundary lifts.** Use a finite boundary partition, graph coordinates `r=x3−h(y)`, with the domain on `r<0`, outward normal `nu=(-grad h,1)/sqrt(1+|grad h|²)`, and a fixed normal cutoff equal to one near 0. On a localized boundary datum `g_j(y,t)`, the Dirichlet lift is `rho(r)g_j(y,t)` with a larger fixed chart cutoff. For an outward conormal datum `kappa_j`, the Neumann lift is

$$L_N\kappa_j(y,r,t)=\frac{r\rho(r)\kappa_j(y,t)}{\epsilon\sqrt{1+|\nabla h(y)|^2}},$$

again with a fixed larger chart cutoff equal to one near the datum support. At `r=0`, the terms from differentiating the coefficient or cutoff vanish because of the factor `r`, while `partial_nu r=sqrt(1+|grad h|²)`; hence `epsilon partial_nu L_N kappa_j=kappa_j`. Add the finite chart pieces. The partition's boundary sum is one, so both lifts have the exact required datum. They are linear, independent of time, smooth in an actual spatial collar × `J`, and their spatial `H^{k+2}` norms are bounded by constants times finite `C^{k+2}` boundary seminorms. Choosing higher seminorm orders is allowed; no sharp boundary Sobolev norm is asserted. For Dirichlet, subtract the lift and apply the earlier zero-lift weak Dirichlet solver plus the exact published higher-order Dirichlet estimate to the source `f+epsilon Delta L_Dg_D`.

**Neumann weak existence and H1 bound.** The earlier weak Neumann lemma accepts the bulk `L2` datum and the bounded boundary trace functional, and proves necessity/sufficiency of componentwise compatibility. Smooth boundary `kappa` defines that bounded functional by Cauchy–Schwarz and the exact published `H1→L2(boundary)` trace theorem. Mean-zero coercivity on each component gives

$$\|u\|_{H^1}\le C_{\Omega,\epsilon}\bigl(\|f\|_2+\|\kappa\|_{L^2(\partial\Omega)}\bigr)$$

for the normalized solution, by testing against it and absorbing the gradient norm. A bounded smooth graph domain has only finitely many components: every bounded open component has boundary in the domain boundary; a finite cover by connected one-sided graph patches meets only finitely many components, and every component meets such a patch. Thus all normalizations and lift/estimate sums are finite. After subtracting `H=L_N kappa`, the residual `w=u−H` has homogeneous Neumann flux and source `f+epsilon Delta H`; its mean is the negative mean of `H`. The smooth first Green identity verifies the weak lift subtraction, and the divergence theorem verifies that its residual bulk integral is zero under the original compatibility. A constant normalization does not affect the flux or elliptic equation.

**Natural-boundary H2 estimate; explicit source terms.** Flatten the fixed smooth boundary and take a localized weak solution `z∈H1` supported away from artificial chart edges, whose weak equation, for supported `H1` tests including nonzero boundary trace, is

$$\int A_{ij}\partial_jz\partial_iv=\int p v+\int G_i\partial_iv,\quad p\in L^2,\ G\in H^1.$$

The smooth symmetric uniformly positive transformed `A` is the ordinary Jacobian/metric transform of the constant scalar operator. The original homogeneous-flux problem has `G=0`; localization by a spatial cutoff `eta` changes the scalar datum to `eta p−A grad z·grad eta+G·grad eta` and the vector datum to `eta G+z A grad eta`, still respectively `L2` and `H1`. These exact terms account for natural flux under localization; no false zero-trace condition is imposed.

For a tangential direction `k`, put `w_h=delta_h^k z` and test with `v=−delta_{−h}^k(eta² w_h)`. This is a supported `H1` test, allowed by the natural variational formulation; it need not vanish at the physical boundary. The published quotient integration-by-parts/product/weak-commutation identities give principal term `integral eta² A(y+h) grad w_h·grad w_h≥alpha||eta grad w_h||²`. The coefficient/cutoff remainders are exactly those of the usual quotient expansion and are bounded by `C||z||H1 (||eta grad w_h||2+||w_h||2)`, with `||w_h||2≤C||z||H1` and `||delta_h A||infinity≤||partial_k A||infinity`. The scalar datum contributes at most `C||p||2(||eta grad w_h||2+||w_h||2)` because the derivative quotient stays on the test, not on `p`. Discrete integration by parts moves the quotient in the vector datum term to `G`, whose contribution is

$$\left|\int\delta_h^kG\cdot\nabla(\eta^2w_h)\right|\le C\|G\|_{H^1}(\|\eta\nabla w_h\|_2+\|w_h\|_2).$$

Cauchy–Schwarz and Young absorption give a uniform bound `||eta grad delta_h^k z||2≤C(||p||2+||G||H1+||z||H1)`. Pass to test pairings; the quotient's limiting derivative is a bounded functional on the `L2` closure of compact tests, and Hilbert Riesz supplies its `L2` representative. This provides all second derivatives with a tangential factor, including mixed ones, without a weak-subsequence assumption. The distributional equation is `−div(A grad z)=p−div G`; therefore the normal derivative has the corrected identity

$$A_{33}\partial_{33}z=-p+\operatorname{div}G-\sum_{(i,j)\ne(3,3)}A_{ij}\partial_{ij}z-\sum_{i,j}(\partial_iA_{ij})\partial_jz.$$

The right side is `L2` and `A33≥alpha>0`, giving the remaining derivative. Interior patches permit all quotient directions. Finite cover and the bounded chart pullbacks give the global natural-boundary `H2` estimate with the displayed data norms and `||w||H1`.

**Every higher order, without pretending Neumann derivatives keep zero flux.** If `w∈H^{k+1}` and its smooth homogeneous-Neumann equation has datum in `H^k`, localize as above; the localized scalar datum lies in `H^k`, and its vector datum lies in `H^{k+1}`. Tangentially differentiate by a multi-index `alpha` of order `k`. The resulting weak identity for `D_tan^alpha z∈H1` keeps principal matrix `A`, with scalar datum `D_tan^alpha p∈L2` and vector datum

$$D_{\rm tan}^\alpha G-\sum_{0<\beta\le\alpha}{\alpha\choose\beta}(D_{\rm tan}^\beta A)\nabla D_{\rm tan}^{\alpha-\beta}z.$$

This vector datum is `H1`: every commutator has at least one coefficient derivative, so it uses derivatives of `z` through at most `k+1`, all available from the induction hypothesis. The coefficient derivatives needed are bounded on the fixed smooth patch. The tangentially differentiated flux need not be zero: it is represented by these vector terms in the **natural weak identity**. The H2 estimate just proved applies to that identity. Tangential testing and differentiation are justified by supported smooth-up-to-boundary approximation; the published half-space extension and whole-space mollification/density interfaces provide the needed `H1` approximants without falsely using `H0^1` density.

This controls order-`k+2` derivatives with at most two normal factors. Expand the strong elliptic equation on the interior of each half-patch, differentiate at total order `k`, and recover successively target derivatives with three, four, ... normal factors by solving for the sole `A33` principal term. Every other derivative of order `k+2` has fewer normal factors; derivatives landing on coefficients use `z` through at most `k+1`. The source derivatives are `L2`. The identities represent global weak derivatives on the open half-patch because every compact test support lies in its interior. Finite cover closes the induction. Thus, for smooth data,

$$\|u\|_{H^{k+2}}\le C_k\bigl(\|f\|_{H^k}+\|\kappa\|_{C^{k+2}(\partial\Omega)}+\|u\|_{H^1}\bigr),$$

where constants include the fixed geometry and `epsilon`. This sufficient, nonsharp estimate is complete for smooth parameter families and does not invoke a nonexistent published Neumann higher-order theorem.

**Strong equation and exact Neumann trace after regularity.** Once the estimates give all spatial orders, Sobolev embedding yields a $C^2$ representative on the closure. The weak equation tested against compact interior smooth functions makes the continuous residual $-\epsilon\Delta u-f$ vanish pointwise: if it had a nonzero value, continuity and a nonnegative bump supported in a small interior ball would give a nonzero test pairing. Apply the first Green identity to the smooth representative and tests obtained from the fixed smooth Dirichlet boundary lift. The weak Neumann identity then gives $\int_{\partial\Omega}(\epsilon\partial_\nu u-\kappa)q=0$ for every smooth boundary test $q$. If that continuous boundary difference were nonzero at some point, a nonnegative chart bump supported where it keeps one strict sign would produce a nonzero boundary integral (the smooth chart area Jacobian is positive). Thus the classical conormal equality is exact. This argument recovers the strong boundary condition from the natural weak formulation rather than presupposing it.

**Joint smoothness and the actual neighbourhood.** Differences and time derivatives of compatible data stay in the same compatible linear data space. Weak H1 continuity follows from the energy estimate. Applying the higher-order estimate to a difference quotient minus the solution for the derivative data makes that error tend to zero in every `H^m` on compact time patches, since bulk derivatives converge in `H^k`, boundary derivatives converge in the finite `C^{k+2}` seminorm, and the H1 error tends to zero. Induction gives all time derivatives as solutions for the differentiated data. Higher-order Sobolev embedding gives one consistent family of all mixed boundary jets; the first new parameter-preserving extension lemma then supplies a single smooth ambient continuation. Dirichlet families follow the same argument with the fixed Dirichlet lift and zero-trace operator. This proves both parameter branches of the second supplier.

supplier_inspections.statement_read:
If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p<\infty$ and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then the compactly supported smooth
functions $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ are dense in
$W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$: for every
$u\in W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ with
$$\|\varphi-u\|_{W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n)}<\delta.$$
No such norm-density assertion is made for $p=\infty$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, be a bounded $C^1$ domain or have the specified finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation. For real $u\in C^2(\overline\Omega)$ and $v\in C^1(\overline\Omega)$, $$\int_\Omega(v\Delta u+Du\cdot Dv)\,dx=\int_{\partial\Omega}v\partial_\nu u\,dS.$$ In the piecewise case the right side is the sum over faces, counted once off E. All integrals are finite.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume Countable Choice for the Sobolev interfaces used by consumers of this
definition. Let $k\ge1$ and $n\ge2$. A **bounded $C^k$ domain** in
$\mathbb R^n$ is a nonempty bounded open set $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ with
the following local graph property. For every boundary point
$x\in\partial\Omega$ there are an open neighbourhood
$W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ of $x$, a rigid motion $R(p)=Qp+b$ with orthogonal
$Q$ and $b\in\mathbb R^n$, an open ball $B\subseteq\mathbb R^{n-1}$, and a
function $h\in C^k(B;\mathbb R)$ such that, after shrinking $W$ so that
$R(W)\subseteq B\times\mathbb R$,
$$R(\Omega\cap W)=R(W)\cap\{(y,s)\in B\times\mathbb R:s<h(y)\}.$$
In the coordinates $z=R(p)$ the domain therefore lies locally strictly below
the graph $s=h(y)$, and the boundary is that graph. The graph convention,
including the requirement that the domain occupy exactly the one-sided
subgraph, is the one of
[[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]; the
regularity $h\in C^k$ is the only strengthening here, and connectedness is not
required.

Write $R(p)=(y,s)$. The **flattening chart** is
$$\Phi:W\longrightarrow\Phi(W)\subseteq B\times\mathbb R,\qquad \Phi(p)=(y,s-h(y)),$$
with inverse $\Phi^{-1}(y,t)=R^{-1}(y,t+h(y))$ on $\Phi(W)$. Thus
$\Phi(\Omega\cap W)=\Phi(W)\cap\{t<0\}$. Both maps are of class $C^k$; the
coordinate shear $(y,s)\mapsto(y,s-h(y))$ has Jacobian determinant one. If
$B'\subset\overline{B'}\subset B$ is a compactly contained concentric ball,
then every derivative $D^\beta h$ with $|\beta|\le k$ is continuous on
$\overline{B'}$, hence bounded there, and consequently the derivatives
through order $k$ of $\Phi$ and of $\Phi^{-1}$ are bounded on the corresponding
compact patch. This is the precise sense in which a boundary chart is said to
have bounded derivatives through order $k$ on the compact patches used; it
does not assert any bound uniform in the chart, the point, or a boundary
atlas.

In dimension $n=1$, the bounded sets satisfying this local one-sided condition
are finite disjoint unions of bounded open intervals. Each endpoint has an
interval neighbourhood on which the domain occupies one side; the coordinate
is the identity or its reflection, and the graph function and derivative
bounds are vacuous. General bounded open subsets of $\mathbb R$ need not have
this property. A bounded $C^1$ domain in the
sense of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]] is a
bounded $C^1$ domain in this sense when $n\ge2$.

This definition asserts no extension theorem, no trace operator, and no
uniformity of chart constants: it fixes only the regularity of the boundary
and the exact one-sided graph convention that later local statements use.

Throughout this surface-integration page assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the earlier Lebesgue and polar measure machinery. Let $n\ge2$. A bounded $C^1$ domain is a nonempty bounded open set $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ whose boundary is locally, after a rigid change of coordinates, the graph $z=h(y)$ of a $C^1$ function, with $\Omega$ locally exactly the subgraph $z<h(y)$. Connectedness is not required. The outward normal in these coordinates is $\nu=(-Dh,1)/\sqrt{1+|Dh|^2}$, transported by the orthogonal coordinate map. Its overlap agreement is justified with surface charts below.

The convention $F\in C^1(\overline\Omega)$ means F is continuously differentiable in $\Omega$, and F and its first derivatives extend continuously to its closure. For $C^2$ require the same for derivatives through order two. No ambient extension across the boundary is required. Derivatives use [[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]]; products are the real Euclidean inner products of [[def-inner-product-space]]. Write $\operatorname{div}F=\sum_i\partial_iF_i$, $Du=(\partial_iu)_i$ and $\Delta u=\sum_i\partial_i^2u$.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. These are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]].

supplier_inspections.statement: Let the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$, its spatial Euclidean structure and its units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $k\ge1$. An electric field of class $C^k$ on the region is a map $E:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that is of class $C^k$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; a magnetic field of class $C^k$ is a map $B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of the same class. At fixed $t\in I$ the maps $E(\cdot,t),B(\cdot,t):\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ are real spatial vector fields on the region $\Omega$, read in the $\delta$-orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the frame. The framework uses: $C^1$ fields in the classical Maxwell branch, $C^2$ fields where second or mixed time-space derivatives of the fields appear, and $C^\infty$ fields in the smooth existence branches; every statement carries its own regularity and no regularity beyond it is asserted. Conventions: (a) $E$ is a polar vector and $B$ an axial vector relative to the orientation of the spatial basis; the changes of inertial description adopted in [[post-sr-inertial-covariance]] are proper and orientation preserving, so orientation-reversing descriptions are not among them; (b) the fields are defined by their values on $\Omega\times I$, and no value at a point of singular source support is asserted; (c) $E$ carries V m$^{-1}$ and $B$ carries T; (d) the identification of the pair $(E,B)$ with the components of an alternating two-form, including its transformation behaviour, is made in [[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]] and is not presupposed here.
supplier_inspections.strategy: An explicit type/domain/convention definition: the fields are maps on the product $\Omega\times I$ of the laboratory region with a stated class of regularity, and their fixed-time readings are spatial vector fields in the frame basis. The regularity notion is that of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; the polar/axial convention and the exclusion of pointwise values at singular source support are conventions recorded explicitly rather than used implicitly. No differential equation and no derived quantity is introduced by this definition.

supplier_inspections.statement: Let $c>0$, let the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ with its restricted inertial chart be that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], let fields and units be those of [[def-em-fields]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]], and let the potential-pair vocabulary (scalar-vector pair, field pair $E(\varphi,A),B(\varphi,A)$, Lorenz divergence $G$, Lorenz gauge, gauge transform $T_\chi$ and wave expression $W$) be that of [[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]] on that region. (a) [Representations] For a field pair $(E,B)$ of class $C^{k-1}$ on $\Omega\times I$ and an integer $k\ge2$, a **potential representation of class $C^k$** of $(E,B)$ is a pair $(\varphi,A)$ of class $C^k$ jointly on $\Omega\times I$ whose field pair is $(E,B)$, that is, $\varphi:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$, $A:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^k$ jointly ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]) with $$E=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA,\qquad B=\operatorname{curl}A\qquad\text{on }\Omega\times I,$$ the derivatives being those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. This definition asserts neither existence (supplied on star-shaped regions under their stated hypotheses by [[pthm-em-spacetime-potentials]]) nor uniqueness of a representation. (b) [Gauge functions and gauge equivalence] A **gauge function** of class $C^m$ ($m\ge2$) on $\Omega\times I$ is a function $\chi:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^m$ jointly; its **gauge transformation** acts on a potential pair by $$T_\chi(\varphi,A):=(\varphi-\partial_t\chi,\ A+\nabla\chi),$$ the transform of a $C^m$ pair being a potential pair of class $C^{m-1}$. Two pairs are **gauge related** when one is the transform of the other by some gauge function. On pairs and generators of class $C^\infty$, $T_0$ is the identity and $T_{\chi_1}(T_{\chi_2}(\varphi,A))=T_{\chi_1+\chi_2}(\varphi,A)$ for all $C^\infty$ generators $\chi_1,\chi_2$ ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], componentwise); hence gauge relatedness is an equivalence relation on the $C^\infty$ potential pairs. (c) [Conditions] A pair is **in Lorenz gauge** on $\Omega\times I$ when $G=\operatorname{div}A+c^{-2}\partial_t\varphi=0$ there, and **in Coulomb gauge** in the chosen spatial chart when $\operatorname{div}A=0$ there. These are properties of a pair in the stated conventions. The existence of a gauge function achieving a condition, with or without prescribed initial or boundary data, is a separate PDE conclusion with its own hypotheses and is not part of this definition. (d) [Physical status] The physical content of a representation is its field pair $(E,B)$ of [[def-em-fields]]; the pair $(\varphi,A)$ and the gauge function are auxiliary, their values are convention dependent, and gauge related representations have the same field pair. The scalar potential carries the volt and the vector potential the tesla metre, consistently with [[def-em-si-conventions]]; no value of $\varphi$ or $A$ is by itself an observable or evidence for a field.
supplier_inspections.strategy:
A vocabulary and bookkeeping definition over the exact interfaces of [[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]]; it makes no existence or solvability claim. Obligations checked: (i) the field-pair formulas and the transform are those of the cited definition, so the regularity statements (a $C^m$ pair gives $C^{m-1}$ fields; a $C^m$ generator gives a $C^{m-1}$ transform) are inherited exactly; (ii) the composition identity is the componentwise linearity of the coordinate partial derivatives, $\partial_t(\chi_1+\chi_2)=\partial_t\chi_1+\partial_t\chi_2$ and $
abla(\chi_1+\chi_2)=
abla\chi_1+
abla\chi_2$ ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]), together with $T_0=\mathrm{id}$; the inverse of $T_\chi$ is $T_{-\chi}$, so the relation is reflexive, symmetric and transitive on $C^\infty$ pairs; (iii) the definition deliberately separates the two gauge conditions from their reachability: no conclusion that a pair can be put in either gauge, with or without prescribed data, is drawn here (compare [[pthm-em-spacetime-potentials]] for existence of representations and the gauge-reachability theorem later on this page for the two declared branches); (iv) no choice principle, no domain hypothesis beyond the laboratory region, and no Maxwell equation is used.

supplier_inspections.statement:
Let $c>0$ and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3	imes\mathbb R$ be open. A **scalar-vector potential pair** of class $C^k$ on $\Omega$ (for an integer $k\ge0$) is a pair $(\varphi,A)$ with $\varphi:\Omega	o\mathbb R$ and $A:\Omega	o\mathbb R^3$ each of class $C^k$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]] (the components of $A$ componentwise). For such a pair with $k\ge1$ its **electric field** and **magnetic field** are $$E(\varphi,A):=-
abla\varphi-\partial_tA,\qquad B(\varphi,A):=\operatorname{curl}A,$$ where $
abla$ is the gradient of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]], $\partial_t$ is the partial derivative of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]] and $\operatorname{curl}$ and $\operatorname{div}$ are those of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]; both $E(\varphi,A)$ and $B(\varphi,A)$ are maps $\Omega	o\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^{k-1}$. For $k\ge1$ the **Lorenz divergence** of the pair is the function $$G(\varphi,A):=\operatorname{div}A+c^{-2}\partial_t\varphi,$$ also of class $C^{k-1}$, and the pair is **in Lorenz gauge** on $\Omega$ when $G(\varphi,A)=0$ throughout $\Omega$. For $k\ge2$ and a $C^k$ function $\chi:\Omega	o\mathbb R$ (a **gauge function**) the **gauge transform** of the pair is $$T_{\chi}(\varphi,A):=(\varphi-\partial_t\chi,\ A+
abla\chi),$$ again a potential pair, of class $C^{k-1}$. Finally, for a $C^2$ function $u:\Omega	o\mathbb R$ put $$Wu:=c^{-2}\partial_t^2u-\Delta u,$$ with $\Delta$ the Laplacian of [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]] and $\partial_t^2$ the second partial derivative in $t$ ([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]); this is the normalization $W=c^{-2}\Box_c$ of the wave operator of speed $c$ of [[def-wave-equation-cauchy-data-and-wave-speed]]. For a $C^2$ map $U:\Omega	o\mathbb R^m$ with components $U_1,\dots,U_m$, one writes $WU:=(WU_1,\dots,WU_m)$ componentwise. Nothing in this definition asserts that a gauge function with prescribed auxiliary data exists, that every potential pair is gauge equivalent to a pair in Lorenz gauge, or that $Wu=g$ is solvable: those are conclusions with their own hypotheses. The signs $-
abla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $A+
abla\chi$, the factor $c^{-2}$ in $G$ and the spelling *Lorenz* are part of the convention.
supplier_inspections.strategy: Vocabulary and regularity audit; a definition asserts no existence theorem. (i) If $\varphi,A$ are $C^k$ then $\nabla\varphi$ and the three partial derivatives $\partial_tA_i$ are $C^{k-1}$ ([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]], [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), so $E(\varphi,A)$ is a $C^{k-1}$ map $\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ and likewise $B(\varphi,A)$ and $G(\varphi,A)$ for $k\ge1$, since the curl and divergence of a $C^1$ field are computed pointwise from first partial derivatives ([[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]). (ii) For a $C^k$ gauge function with $k\ge2$, $\partial_t\chi$ and $\nabla\chi$ are $C^{k-1}$, so $T_\chi(\varphi,A)$ is a pair of class $C^{k-1}$. (iii) The wave expression is the stated normalization: [[def-wave-equation-cauchy-data-and-wave-speed]] fixes $\Box_c=\partial_t^2-c^2\Delta$, so $c^{-2}\Box_c=c^{-2}\partial_t^2-\Delta=W$, and $\Delta$ is the Laplacian of [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]. (iv) No solvability is asserted: existence of $\chi$ with $W\chi=G$ is supplied later on this page under slab hypotheses, and it carries the Axiom of Countable Choice through the cited wave theorem. The definition is stated on an arbitrary open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ so that both the full slab and complements of worldlines are instances.

supplier_inspections.statement_read:
Assume Countable Choice for the Sobolev interfaces used below. Let
$\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with $n\ge1$, let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let
$u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
([[def-locally-integrable-function-as-a-regular-distribution]]). For
$h\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$ and $i\in\{1,\dots,n\}$ let $e_i$ be the
$i$-th standard unit vector and put
$$\Omega_{i,h}:=\{x\in\Omega:x+he_i\in\Omega\}=\Omega\cap(\Omega-he_i),$$
an open subset of $\Omega$, since it is the intersection of the open set
$\Omega$ with the preimage of $\Omega$ under the homeomorphism
$x\mapsto x+he_i$. The **$i$-th difference quotient of $u$ of size $h$** is
$$\delta_h^iu(x):=\frac{u(x+he_i)-u(x)}{h},\qquad x\in\Omega_{i,h},$$
read on the almost-everywhere classes
([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]); the
**difference-quotient vector** is
$$\delta_hu:=(\delta_h^1u,\dots,\delta_h^nu),$$
defined on the open intersection $\Omega_h:=\bigcap_{i=1}^n\Omega_{i,h}$,
while each component is defined on its own shrunken set $\Omega_{i,h}$.

Throughout this page the translation notation is the published one of
[[def-translation-of-a-function-on-rn]], namely
$\tau_hu(x)=u(x-h)$; consequently the forward shift that occurs in the
product rule is the translate by $-he_i$:
$$u(x+he_i)=(\tau_{-he_i}u)(x),\qquad \delta_h^iu=\frac{\tau_{-he_i}u-u}{h}\quad\text{on }\Omega_{i,h}.$$

For the open upper half-space
$H=\{x_n>0\}$ and a **tangential**
index $j<n$, the translation $x\mapsto x+he_j$ maps $H$ onto $H$; hence
$\delta_h^ju$ is defined on all of $H$. For the **normal** index $n$ and
$h>0$ one has $H_{n,h}=H$ (since $x_n>0$ implies $x_n+h>0$), while for
$h<0$ one has $H_{n,h}=\{x\in H:x_n>|h|\}$, a proper subset of $H$.

**Well-definedness.** Both values $u(x)$ and $u(x+he_i)$ in the numerator are
defined for every $x\in\Omega_{i,h}$, and
$$|\delta_h^iu(x)|\le\frac{|u(x+he_i)|+|u(x)|}{|h|},$$
so $\delta_h^iu\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega_{i,h};\mathbb K)$: on a compact
$K\Subset\Omega_{i,h}$ the first term is controlled by
$\int_K|u(x+he_i)|\,dx=\int_{K+he_i}|u(y)|\,dy<\infty$, because
$K+he_i$ is a compact subset of $\Omega$, and the second term is controlled
on $K\Subset\Omega$. Further, the definition depends only on the class of
$u$: if $u=\widetilde u$ almost everywhere on $\Omega$ and $E\subseteq\Omega$
is a null set with $u=\widetilde u$ on $\Omega\setminus E$, then
$\delta_h^iu\ne\delta_h^i\widetilde u$ only at points of
$(\Omega_{i,h}\cap E)\cup(\Omega_{i,h}\cap(E-he_i))$, a null set because
$E$ is null and $E-he_i$ is null by the choice-free translation invariance of
Lebesgue measure
([[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-and-measurability-are-translation-invariant]]).

**Two warnings, part of the definition.** First, a difference quotient is
defined on the shrunken set $\Omega_{i,h}$ inside $\Omega$, which may equal
$\Omega$ when the shift preserves it; in particular it may be undefined on a strip of width $|h|$
along the boundary, so no estimate below differentiates a Sobolev class
across the boundary. Second, extending a class $u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$ by zero
does not enlarge the domain of its difference quotient: the quotient of the
extension agrees with $\delta_h^iu$ on $\Omega_{i,h}$, while values outside
$\Omega_{i,h}$ use points not both in $\Omega$ and are not values of the
original quotient. In the upper half-space, $\Omega_{n,h}=H$ for $h>0$,
whereas $\Omega_{n,h}=\{x\in H:x_n>|h|\}$ for $h<0$. This is why every
boundary argument on this page uses only
tangential quotients of compactly supported localisations, for which the
shrunken domain is the whole half-space and no extension across
$\partial\Omega$ is invoked.

Let $a \in \mathbb{R}$, where $\mathbb{R}$ is the ambient ordered field
([[def-ordered-field]], [[def-field]]).

**Natural exponents.** By the recursion theorem ([[thm-recursion]]) applied to
the set $\mathbb{R}$, the starting element $1$ and the function
$f(x) = x \cdot a$, there is a unique function $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$,
written $n \mapsto a^n$, with

$$a^0 = 1, \qquad a^{n+1} = a^n \cdot a \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

Thus $a^1 = a$, $a^2 = a \cdot a$, and so on. Note that this is defined for
**every** $a$, including $a = 0$.

**Negative exponents.** If $a \ne 0$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, set

$$a^{-n} := (a^n)^{-1}.$$

**Why that is legitimate.** The right-hand side presupposes that $a^n$ is
invertible, that is, that $a^n \ne 0$. This is a proof obligation and not an
observation, and it is discharged by claim 2 of [[lem-power-laws]]: for $a \ne 0$
in a field, $a^n \ne 0$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, proved there by induction on
$n$ from the fact that a field has no zero divisors ([[lem-of-no-zero-divisors]]).
That lemma is a statement *about* the operation introduced here, so it depends on
this definition and is recorded in this item's `justified_by` rather than in its
`deps` (SCHEMA §3). Given $a^n \ne 0$, the value $(a^n)^{-1}$ is a single
well-determined element, because multiplicative inverses in a field are unique
([[lem-of-inverse-unique]]).

**Integer exponents.** Every integer $m$ ([[def-integers]]) is either
$\iota(n)$ or $-\iota(n)$ for a unique natural $n$, where $\iota$ is the
embedding $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z}$ ([[lem-nat-embeds-int]],
[[def-int-operations]]). This too is a citation and not a slogan: the order on
$\mathbb{Z}$ is total ([[thm-int-ordered-ring]]), so $m \ge 0$ or $m < 0$; the
image of $\iota$ is exactly the set of nonnegative integers, and each of them is
$\iota(n)$ for a unique natural $n$ ([[lem-nat-embeds-int]]); and if $m < 0$ then
$-m > 0$, by compatibility of the order with addition ([[thm-int-ordered-ring]]),
so $-m = \iota(n)$ and $m = -\iota(n)$, with $n$ unique because $\iota$ is
injective. The two clauses above therefore define $a^m$ for every
$m \in \mathbb{Z}$ whenever $a \ne 0$, and for every $m \in \mathbb{N}$ for
arbitrary $a$. The clauses are consistent where they overlap: the only overlap is
$m = 0$, where $-\iota(0) = \iota(0)$ and $(a^0)^{-1} = 1^{-1} = 1 = a^0$.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) with its order
([[def-real-order]]).

A subset $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is **order-convex** when

$$x, y \in I \text{ and } x \le z \le y \;\Longrightarrow\; z \in I .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$:

| | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ |
| $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ |
| $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ |
| $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ |
| | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |

An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is
for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is
**closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$,
$[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$. The forms $[a,b)$ and
$(a,b]$ are **half-open**.

**The symbols $\pm\infty$ are notation and not elements of $\mathbb{R}$.** They
mark which side carries no endpoint condition at all; the five forms in the right
column are defined by the displayed conditions on $x$ alone, and no arithmetic is
ever performed with $\infty$. This is the same refusal to extend $\mathbb{R}$
silently that [[rem-sup-conventions]] records for suprema.

**Every one of the nine forms is order-convex.** Each is defined by a conjunction
of at most two conditions, each of the shape $a < x$, $a \le x$, $x < b$ or
$x \le b$, and each such condition is inherited by an intermediate point: if
$a < x$ and $x \le z$ then $a < z$, and if $z \le y$ and $y < b$ then $z < b$,
by transitivity of the order ([[def-ordered-field]]). Applying this to whichever
one or two conditions define the form in question gives $z \in I$ whenever
$x, y \in I$ and $x \le z \le y$.

**Bounded intervals.** An interval is **bounded** ([[def-bounded-set]]) exactly
when it is of one of the four forms in the left column: for those, $a$ is a lower
bound and $b$ an upper bound. The other five forms are unbounded, on the side or
sides written with $\infty$; the verification is in the remarks below.

**Nondegeneracy.** An interval is **degenerate** when it has at most one element,
and **nondegenerate** when it has at least two. For the four bounded forms with
endpoints $a$ and $b$:

- $[a,b]$ is nonempty exactly when $a \le b$, and it is nondegenerate exactly
  when $a < b$. It is the singleton $\{a\}$ when $a = b$.
- $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are nonempty exactly when $a < b$, and then each
  is nondegenerate.

The only assertion here that is not immediate from the defining conditions is
that $a < b$ makes $(a,b)$ nonempty with at least two points. It holds because
$a < (a+b)/2 < b$, which follows from $a < b$ by adding $a$, respectively $b$, to
both sides and halving ([[def-ordered-field]]); repeating the halving inside
$(a, (a+b)/2)$ produces a second point.

**Closed bounded intervals.** These are the sets $[a,b]$ with $a \le b$, which is
exactly the condition making them nonempty. They are the intervals the nested
interval property is stated for, and the phrase *closed bounded interval* always
carries the hypothesis $a \le b$ in this library.

**Length.** The **length** of a bounded interval presented by its endpoints
$a \le b$ is

$$\ell = b - a \;\ge\; 0 .$$

Length is attached to the presentation by endpoints and is not recovered from the
set: $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are all empty when $a = b$, and so is
$(c,c)$ for any other $c$, while each of these presentations has length $0$, so
nothing inconsistent arises; but the endpoints are named explicitly at every
point where a length is used in this library, and never inferred from the set.
Unbounded intervals are assigned no length.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$ in the sense of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. Then $\nabla f$ is a $C^1$ field on $U$ by [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], since each of its components $\partial_if$ has continuous first partial derivatives, so its divergence is defined; the **Laplacian** of $f$ is

$$\Delta f:=\operatorname{div}\nabla f=\sum_{i<n}\partial_i\partial_if,$$

with the gradient of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]] and the divergence of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]. A $C^2$ function with $\Delta f=0$ on $U$ is called **harmonic** on $U$.

For a $C^2$ map $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{q-1}):U\to\mathbb R^q$, whose components are $C^2$ by [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], $\Delta F$ is the field whose $i$th coordinate is $\Delta F_i$. In the three-coordinate naming of this page, $\Delta f=\partial_x\partial_xf+\partial_y\partial_yf+\partial_z\partial_zf$ and $\Delta F=(\Delta F_x,\Delta F_y,\Delta F_z)$.

A **formal real polynomial** is either the zero polynomial $0$, or a finite coefficient list $(a_0,\ldots,a_n)$ with $a_n\ne0$; we write the latter as $p(X)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}a_kX^k$. The list, rather than the function it induces, is the polynomial object. Its **evaluation** at $x\in\mathbb R$ is the real number $p(x):=\sum_{k=0}^{n}a_kx^k$.

For nonzero $p=(a_0,\ldots,a_n)$, define $\deg p:=n$ and $\operatorname{lc}(p):=a_n$. The zero polynomial has no degree and no leading coefficient. A nonzero polynomial is **monic** when $\operatorname{lc}(p)=1$. Thus degree and leading coefficient are defined from the displayed finite list, without asserting that distinct formal polynomials define distinct functions. The conventions for finite sums and integer powers used in the evaluation are recorded in [[def-finite-sum]], [[def-integer-power]].

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field ([[def-real-numbers]]) and
a **sequence of reals** is a function $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$
([[def-sequence]]), written $(a_k)$; recall that $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$.

**Partial sums.** Let $(a_k)$ be a sequence of reals. Its **sequence of partial
sums** is

$$s_n \;:=\; \sum_{k < n} a_k \qquad (n \in \mathbb{N}),$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. In particular $s_0 = 0$, the empty sum, and
$s_{n+1} = s_n + a_n$ for every $n$, those being exactly the two recursion clauses
that define the finite sum. Note that $s_n$ is the sum of the $n$ terms
$a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$, so the index $n$ counts terms rather than naming the last
one.

**Convergence, the sum, divergence.** The **series** of $(a_k)$, written
$\sum a_k$, **converges** when the sequence $(s_n)$ of partial sums converges
([[def-real-limit]]), and then the **sum of the series** is

$$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} a_k \;:=\; \lim_{n} s_n .$$

The series **diverges** when $(s_n)$ does not converge. A convergent sequence of
reals has exactly one limit ([[lem-limit-unique]]), so the displayed symbol names
a single real number and nothing further has to be checked for it to be
well defined.

**Series with a general starting index.** Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $a$ be a
function on $\{\, k \in \mathbb{N} : k \ge m \,\}$, which we call a **family from
$m$** and write $(a_k)_{k \ge m}$. The series

$$\sum_{k \ge m} a_k$$

is by definition the series of the sequence $b_j := a_{j + m}$,
$j \in \mathbb{N}$, which is a genuine sequence of reals; it converges exactly
when that series converges, and its sum is then written
$\sum_{k = m}^{\infty} a_k$. Its partial sums are

$$\sum_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k \;=\; \sum_{j < n-m} a_{m+j} \qquad (n \ge m),$$

in the notation of [[def-finite-sum]], the value at $n = m$ being the empty sum
$0$. A sequence on $\mathbb{N}$ is the case $m = 0$, and the two readings of
$\sum a_k$ agree there, since $b_j = a_j$.

**This clause is not a convenience.** Sequences in this library are functions on
$\mathbb{N}$ and $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$ ([[def-sequence]]), while many of the
classical series are built from expressions that are undefined at the index $0$:
$1/k$, $1/k^{p}$ and $|a_k|^{1/k}$ all require $k \ge 1$. Writing such a series as
$\sum_{k \ge 1} a_k$ names an honest object, whereas writing it as a sequence on
$\mathbb{N}$ would require a value at an index where the defining expression has
none. Every statement on this page says which starting index it uses.

**Tail series.** For $N \in \mathbb{N}$, the **$N$-th tail series** of
$\sum a_k$ is $\sum_{k \ge N} a_k$, that is the series of the $N$-th tail
$a^{(N)}$ of [[def-sequence]], whose terms are $a^{(N)}_j = a_{j+N}$. The
$0$-th tail series is the series itself.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

A nonempty open set $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ is **star-shaped with respect to** $a\in U$ when

$$a+t(x-a)\in U\qquad\text{for every }x\in U\text{ and }0\le t\le1.$$

The point $a$ is a **star centre**. Every convex open set of [[def-convex-subset-of-euclidean-space]] is star-shaped with respect to each of its points. The nonemptiness and the chosen centre are part of the definition.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $k\ge1$, $1\le p\le\infty$ and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open
and let $\Phi:U\to V$ be a $C^k$ diffeomorphism with inverse
$\Psi:=\Phi^{-1}:V\to U$. Fix open sets $U_0\subset\subset U$ and
$V_0\subset\subset V$ with $\Phi(U_0)\subseteq V_0$, and suppose that on
$\overline{U_0}$ the derivatives of $\Phi$ through order $k$ are bounded and
that on $\overline{V_0}$ the derivatives of $\Psi$ through order $k$ are
bounded; in the situation of
[[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]] these are exactly the compact
patches on which the flattening chart and its inverse have bounded derivatives
through order $k$. Then:

1. for every $u\in W^{k,p}(V_0;\mathbb K)$ the composition
$u\circ\Phi$ belongs to $W^{k,p}(U_0;\mathbb K)$, and for every
$1\le|\alpha|\le k$ its weak derivatives satisfy, almost everywhere on
$U_0$,
$$D^\alpha(u\circ\Phi)=\sum_{1\le|\beta|\le|\alpha|}\bigl((D^\beta u)\circ\Phi\bigr)\,P_{\alpha\beta}\bigl(D\Phi,\dots,D^k\Phi\bigr),$$
where $P_{\alpha\beta}$ is a universal polynomial with integer coefficients,
whose values on $\overline{U_0}$ are bounded by a constant depending only on
$n,k$ and the stated bounds for $\Phi$;

2. there is a constant $C$, depending only on $n$, $k$, $p$ and the two sets of
chart bounds, with
$$\|u\circ\Phi\|_{W^{k,p}(U_0)}\le C\,\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(V_0)}\qquad\text{for all }u\in W^{k,p}(V_0;\mathbb K).$$
If in addition $\Psi(V_0)\subseteq U_0$ (equivalently, under the stated
$\Phi(U_0)\subseteq V_0$, $\Phi(U_0)=V_0$), the same assertion holds for
composition with $\Psi$ from $W^{k,p}(U_0)$ to $W^{k,p}(V_0)$.

For $k=1$ only the first derivatives of $\Phi$ and $\Psi$ enter, so bounded
$C^1$ chart and inverse data suffice; no $C^1$-only claim is made for $k>1$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with $n\ge1$,
let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let
$u,v\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, and fix $h\ne0$ and
$i\in\{1,\dots,n\}$. Write
$\Omega_{i,h}=\{x\in\Omega:x+he_i\in\Omega\}$ and
$\Omega_{i,-h}=\{x\in\Omega:x-he_i\in\Omega\}$
([[def-first-difference-quotient]]), so that
$\Omega_{i,-h}=\Omega_{i,h}+he_i$. Then:

(i) **Integration by parts, two-domain form.** Whenever the displayed
integrals converge absolutely,
$$\int_{\Omega_{i,h}}\delta_h^iu\,v\,dx=-\int_{\Omega_{i,-h}}u\,\delta_{-h}^iv\,dx+\frac1h\Big(\int_{\Omega_{i,-h}}uv\,dx-\int_{\Omega_{i,h}}uv\,dx\Big).$$
Consequently, if
$$\int_{\Omega_{i,h}}uv\,dx=\int_{\Omega_{i,-h}}uv\,dx,$$
in particular if $uv$ vanishes almost everywhere outside
$\Omega_{i,h}\cap\Omega_{i,-h}$ — for instance when $uv$ has compact support in
$\Omega$ and $|h|<\operatorname{dist}(\operatorname{supp}(uv),\partial\Omega)$
— or if $\Omega_{i,h}=\Omega_{i,-h}$, then
$\int_{\Omega_{i,h}}\delta_h^iu\,v\,dx=-\int_{\Omega_{i,-h}}u\,\delta_{-h}^iv\,dx$,
with the integrals taken over their respective shrunken sets. For $\Omega=\mathbb R^n$
and $u\in L^p(\Omega)$, $v\in L^{p'}(\Omega)$ with $1\le p\le\infty$ and
$p'$ the Hölder conjugate exponent of [[def-conjugate-exponents]]
($1/p+1/p'=1$), both sides are absolutely convergent and
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n}\delta_h^iu\,v\,dx=-\int_{\mathbb R^n}u\,\delta_{-h}^iv\,dx.$$

(ii) **Product rule.** If $uv\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$, then a.e. on
$\Omega_{i,h}$,
$$\delta_h^i(uv)=\big(\tau_{-he_i}u\big)\,\delta_h^iv+\big(\delta_h^iu\big)\,v=u\,\delta_h^iv+\big(\delta_h^iu\big)\big(\tau_{-he_i}v\big),$$
with the translation $\tau_{-he_i}$ of [[def-translation-of-a-function-on-rn]].
The identity is a pointwise a.e. algebraic identity; no local integrability of
its shifted cross-products is asserted beyond the hypothesis $uv\in L^1_{\rm loc}$,
which makes the left side well defined.

(iii) **Commutation with weak derivatives.** If $u$ and all its weak
derivatives $D^\gamma u$ with $|\gamma|\le|\alpha|$ have locally integrable
representatives on $\Omega$
([[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]), then
$$D^\alpha(\delta_h^iu)=\delta_h^i(D^\alpha u)\qquad\text{weakly on }\Omega_{i,h}.$$

All identities are identities of almost-everywhere classes
([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), and the proof uses no
choice beyond the Sobolev interfaces.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F,G:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$, let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$ and let $a,b\in\mathbb R$. Then $aF+bG$ and $fF$ are $C^1$ on $U$ and

$$\operatorname{div}(aF+bG)=a\operatorname{div}F+b\operatorname{div}G,$$

$$\operatorname{div}(fF)=\langle\nabla f,F\rangle+f\operatorname{div}F.$$

If moreover $n=3$, then

$$\operatorname{curl}(aF+bG)=a\operatorname{curl}F+b\operatorname{curl}G,\qquad \operatorname{curl}(fF)=\nabla f\times F+f\operatorname{curl}F.$$

Here $\operatorname{div}$, $\operatorname{curl}$ and the coordinate naming are those of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]], $\nabla f$ is the gradient of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]], $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ is the inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and $\times$ is the cross product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]].

supplier_inspections.statement: Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), carried through [[thm-em-wave-cauchy-kirchhoff]] and its sphere integrations ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $c>0$, $t_0<T$, and let $(\varphi,A)$ be a potential pair of class $C^\infty$ on the slab $Q:=\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]$ in the extension sense of [[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]]: $\varphi$ and $A$ are restrictions of $C^\infty$ functions on $\mathbb R^3\times J$ for some open interval $J\supset[t_0,T]$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). Put $G:=G(\varphi,A)=\operatorname{div}A+c^{-2}\partial_t\varphi$ and $W=c^{-2}\partial_t^2-\Delta$. Then: (a) there is a gauge function $\chi:\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^\infty$ in the extension sense with $\chi(\cdot,t_0)=0$, $\partial_t\chi(\cdot,t_0)=0$ and $W\chi=G$ on $\mathbb R^3\times(t_0,T)$; (b) the gauge-transformed pair $T_\chi(\varphi,A)=(\varphi-\partial_t\chi,\,A+\nabla\chi)$ is again of class $C^\infty$ in the extension sense and its fields are unchanged: $$E(T_\chi(\varphi,A))=E(\varphi,A),\qquad B(T_\chi(\varphi,A))=B(\varphi,A)\qquad\text{on }Q;$$ (c) the transformed pair is in Lorenz gauge: $G(T_\chi(\varphi,A))=G-W\chi=0$ on $\mathbb R^3\times(t_0,T)$; (d) if $\chi_1,\chi_2$ are of class $C^2$ on $Q$ in the extension sense and $W\chi_1=W\chi_2=G$ on $\mathbb R^3\times(t_0,T)$, then $W(\chi_1-\chi_2)=0$ on $\mathbb R^3\times(t_0,T)$. Nothing is asserted about prescribed boundary values of $\chi$ on a bounded spatial domain, about spatial decay of $\chi$, or about Lorenz gauge fixing for a cavity problem with prescribed boundary data; the older global gauge promise on bounded domains is outside this result.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and star-shaped with centre $a$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval, let $k\ge1$, and let $B:U\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be of class $C^k$ jointly with $\operatorname{div}B(\cdot,t)=0$ for every $t$. Then the radial witness $A(x,t):=\int_0^1s\,B(a+s(x-a),t)\times(x-a)\,ds$ is $C^k$ jointly on $U\times I$ and $\operatorname{curl}A(\cdot,t)=B(\cdot,t)$ for every $t$. If in addition $C:U\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ is $C^k$ jointly with $\operatorname{curl}C(\cdot,t)=0$ for every $t$, then the radial scalar witness $\phi(x,t):=\int_0^1\langle C(a+s(x-a),t),x-a\rangle\,ds$ is $C^k$ jointly on $U\times I$ and $\nabla\phi(\cdot,t)=-C(\cdot,t)$ for every $t$. For $C^\infty$ data both potentials are $C^\infty$ jointly. No global potential on an arbitrary open set is claimed.
supplier_inspections.strategy: Repeat the compact-rectangle parameter-differentiation argument for every derivative through order $k$; the parameter derivatives are continuous on the compact rectangle $[0,1]\times$-slices, so the radial witness is $C^k$ jointly. The scalar clause applies the published Poincaré lemma and its radial witness. On a ball the construction is local even when $U$ has holes; first and second cohomological obstructions must not be conflated.

supplier_inspections.statement:
Let $\Omega\subseteq(-L,L)^3$ be bounded and open, let $\varepsilon$ be a measurable symmetric real $3	imes3$ matrix field on $\Omega$ with $\alpha|\xi|^2\le\xi\cdot\varepsilon(x)\xi\le eta|\xi|^2$ for a.e. $x$ and all $\xi\in\mathbb R^3$, $0<\alpha\le eta<\infty$, let $G\in H^1(\Omega)$ be a specified lift, and let $F\in(H_0^1(\Omega))^*$ be bounded. Then there is exactly one $u\in G+H_0^1(\Omega)$ with $$\int_\Omega
abla v\cdot\varepsilon
abla u=F(v)\qquad	ext{for every }v\in H_0^1(\Omega),$$ where $H_0^1=W_0^{1,2}$ carries the gradient norm. For $F(v)=\int_\Omegaho v$ with $ho\in L^2(\Omega)$ this is the weak Poisson solution $-\operatorname{div}(\varepsilon
abla u)=ho$, with the homogeneous boundary datum represented by membership of $H_0^1$ rather than by an unproved classical trace. No boundary datum outside the specified lift class is assumed attainable; classical boundary regularity, general Neumann lifts and transmission regularity remain later obligations.
supplier_inspections.strategy:
On $H_0^1$ the gradient norm is equivalent to the full $H^1$ norm and $H_0^1$ is complete ([[lem-em-zero-boundary-coercivity]]). Put $a(w,v)=\int_\Omega
abla v\cdot\varepsilon
abla w$ and $\ell(v)=F(v)-a(G,v)$ for $v,w\in H_0^1$. The coefficient bounds and Cauchy-Schwarz ([[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]]) make $a$ a bounded symmetric bilinear form with $a(v,v)\ge\alpha\|
abla v\|_2^2$, and $\ell$ is bounded because $F$ is bounded and $a(G,\cdot)$ is controlled by $ eta\|
abla G\|_2\|
abla\cdot\|_2$. The symmetric coercive variational solver ([[lem-em-symmetric-coercive-variational-solver]]) gives a unique $w$ with $a(w,v)=\ell(v)$ for all $v$, and $u=G+w$ solves the stated problem; testing with compactly supported smooth $v$ gives the distributional equation by the weak first-derivative identity. For $F(v)=\intho v$ with $ho\in L^2$, the bound $|F(v)|\le\|ho\|_2\|v\|_2\le2L\|ho\|_2\|
abla v\|_2$ ([[lem-em-zero-boundary-coercivity]], [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]]) makes $F$ bounded, so the existence conclusion applies. Across finitely many material interfaces the weak equation encodes flux continuity where one-sided classical traces exist, by integration by parts on each side.

supplier_inspections.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice (used through the smooth-up-to-the-boundary density theorem below) and the Axiom of Countable Choice (declared by the flattening and Sobolev suppliers). Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded connected $C^1$ domain in the graph sense ([[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]], [[def-connected-space]]); its closure is compact, so the boundary has a finite cover by boundary charts ([[def-compact-space]]). There is a constant $C_\Omega$, depending only on $\Omega$, with $$\|v-v_\Omega\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\le C_\Omega\,\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\qquad\text{for every }v\in H^1(\Omega),\qquad v_\Omega:=\frac1{|\Omega|}\int_\Omega v\,dx .$$ Here $H^1(\Omega)=W^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ with the weak coordinate derivatives, and $\nabla v$ denotes the weak gradient. The estimate is the mean-zero (Poincare) inequality needed for weak Neumann solvability, where the mean-zero subspace carries the gradient norm.
supplier_inspections.strategy:
On a rectangular box $R$ the one-dimensional fundamental theorem along coordinate segments with Cauchy-Schwarz ([[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]]) gives $\int_R\int_R|v(x)-v(y)|^2dx\,dy\le C_R|R|\int_R|
abla v|^2dx$; replacing $x$ by $y$ one coordinate at a time bounds the squared finite sum by three times the sum of the three one-coordinate differences, and Fubini-Tonelli ([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]], [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]) integrates the remaining coordinates. Jensen's inequality ([[thm-finite-jensen-inequality]]) against the normalised $y$-integral gives the local mean estimate $\int_R|v-v_R|^2\le C'_R\int_R|
abla v|^2$. The same argument applies to a half-box. Each boundary graph chart is flattened to a half-box; the $C^k$ boundary flattening lemma ([[lem-c-k-boundary-flattening-preserves-wkp-locally]]) transports the estimate to the chart patch, initially for smooth functions and then for $H^1$ functions by the smooth-up-to-the-boundary density theorem ([[thm-smooth-up-to-the-boundary-density-on-smooth-domains]]), with bounded chart Jacobians and first derivatives. Interior balls are replaced by boxes contained in $\Omega$. Compactness of the boundary and of the residual interior region gives a finite connected cover $\Omega= igcup_jU_j$ with every $|U_j|>0$ and a connected intersection graph: otherwise the finite disjoint unions of graph components would be nonempty relatively open sets partitioning the connected $\Omega$ ([[def-connected-space]]). Writing $a_j$ for the mean of $v$ on $U_j$, the local estimates give $\|v-a_j\|_{L^2(U_j)}\le C_j\|
abla v\|_{L^2(U_j)}$, and the mean differences $|a_j-a_k|$ over nonempty overlaps are bounded by the local gradient energy along a finite spanning tree of the intersection graph. Summing the local squared bounds and the squared mean differences over the finite cover, and using that the global mean minimises $a\mapsto\int_\Omega|v-a|^2$, gives the stated bound.

supplier_inspections.statement:
Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded connected $C^1$ domain, let $\varepsilon$ be measurable symmetric uniformly elliptic, let $ho\in L^2(\Omega)$, and let $g\in H^{-1/2}(\partial\Omega)$, the bounded real dual of the boundary trace space ([[def-fractional-sobolev-space-on-a-compact-c-one-boundary]]). Define $\ell(v)=\int_\Omegaho v+\langle g,Tvangle$ on $H^1(\Omega)$ ([[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]]). A weak Neumann solution is a $u\in H^1$ with $$\int_\Omega
abla v\cdot\varepsilon
abla u=\ell(v)\qquad	ext{for every }v\in H^1(\Omega).$$ Such a solution exists if and only if $\ell(1)=0$, and is then unique up to an additive constant; normalising $\int_\Omega u=0$ makes it unique. On finitely many connected components the compatibility and normalisation are imposed separately on each component. For finitely many disjoint smooth stationary interfaces with piecewise smooth uniformly elliptic $\varepsilon$, bulk data $ho\in L^2$ and prescribed sheet charge $\sigma$ on the interfaces defining a bounded trace functional on $H^1$ (for instance $\sigma\in L^2$ of each smooth compact interface), the same argument gives weak Dirichlet or compatible Neumann existence for the transmission problem, with the globally $H^1$ potential having identical one-sided trace; where the solution is classically smooth on each side, integration by parts gives the jump $n\cdot[\varepsilon
abla u]=-\sigma$, equivalently $n\cdot[D]=\sigma$. General piecewise classical regularity remains a separate requirement.
supplier_inspections.strategy: The trace bound of the prescribed-data lemma and Holder's inequality make $|\ell(v)|\le C\|v\|_{H^1}$ ([[lem-em-prescribed-fractional-dirichlet-existence]], [[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]], [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]]). Testing the equation with $v=1$ makes $\ell(1)=0$ necessary. The mean-zero subspace of $H^1$ is closed, and the mean-zero coercivity lemma makes its gradient norm equivalent to the complete $H^1$ norm ([[lem-em-mean-zero-coercivity-on-a-c-one-domain]]); the symmetric coercive variational solver ([[lem-em-symmetric-coercive-variational-solver]]) solves the coercive symmetric form there. Every $v\in H^1$ is its mean-zero part plus a constant, and the constant term contributes zero on both sides by compatibility, so this solves the full problem; for the difference of two solutions tested against itself the gradient vanishes, and the mean-zero inequality makes the difference constant. Each finite disjoint component is treated separately. The transmission case replaces $\ell$ by the sum of the bulk, boundary and interface trace functionals of the prescribed sheet charge; the same variational argument applies, and the one-sided trace identity holds for the globally $H^1$ potential by trace continuity in each chart, giving the stated jump relation where the solution is classically smooth on each side.

supplier_inspections.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice as declared by the Sobolev completeness theorem ([[thm-sobolev-spaces-are-banach-spaces]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\Omega\subseteq(-L,L)^3$ be bounded and open, and write $H^1(\Omega)=W^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ with $H_0^1(\Omega):=W_0^{1,2}(\Omega)$ the closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ in the $W^{1,2}$ norm ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], [[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]). Then $H^1(\Omega)$ and its closed subspace $H_0^1(\Omega)$ are complete, the quadratic integral norm is a Hilbert norm (its coordinate $L^2$ inner products satisfy the parallelogram law), and $$\|v\|_{L^2}^2\le(2L)^2\,\|\partial_1v\|_{L^2}^2\le(2L)^2\,\|\nabla v\|_{L^2}^2\qquad\text{for every }v\in H_0^1(\Omega). $$ In particular the gradient seminorm is equivalent to the full $H^1$ norm on $H_0^1$, and the argument needs neither a smooth domain nor a general boundary-trace theorem.
supplier_inspections.strategy: For $v\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ extend $v$ by zero to the box $(-L,L)^3$ (legitimate because $\Omega\subseteq(-L,L)^3$). Along each coordinate line the Newton-Leibniz formula ([[thm-newton-leibniz-with-interior-derivative]]) gives $v(x_1,x_2,x_3)=\int_{-L}^{x_1}\partial_1v(s,x_2,x_3)\,ds$; Cauchy-Schwarz for $L^2$ ([[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]]) gives $|v|^2\le2L\int_{-L}^{L}|\partial_1v|^2ds$, and integrating in the other coordinates and then in $x_1$ over a length-$2L$ interval gives $\|v\|_2^2\le(2L)^2\|\partial_1v\|_2^2$, hence the displayed squared inequality with $(2L)^2$ and the nonsquared bound $\|v\|_2\le2L\|\nabla v\|_2$. Approximation in the $W^{1,2}$ norm (the definition of $H_0^1$ as a closure, [[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]) passes both the inequality and the equivalences to all of $H_0^1$ by continuity of the $L^2$ norm; completeness is the Sobolev completeness theorem ([[thm-sobolev-spaces-are-banach-spaces]]) restricted to the closed subspace, and the Hilbert-norm claim follows because the $W^{1,2}$ quadratic norm is induced by the coordinate $L^2$ inner products, which satisfy the parallelogram law.

supplier_inspections.statement_read: Under the page measure convention, if a finite family of open sets $U_j\subset\mathbb R^n$ covers compact K, there are smooth nonnegative $\chi_j$ with compact support in $U_j$ such that $\sum_j\chi_j=1$ on a neighborhood of K. These are ambient smooth functions, also when K is only a $C^1$ hypersurface.

Let $a, b$ be elements of a field ([[def-field]]) and let integer powers be as in
[[def-integer-power]].

1. For all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$: $a^{m+n} = a^m a^n$, $(a^m)^n = a^{mn}$ and $(ab)^n = a^n b^n$.
2. If $a \ne 0$ then $a^n \ne 0$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, and $a^{-m} = (a^m)^{-1}$ for every $m \in \mathbb{Z}$ ([[def-int-operations]]).
